Know Before You Land

A little bit about Bali

via Wikimedia Commons (placeholder)
Where
An island province of Indonesia, between Java and Lombok. You'll be based in Candidasa, on the quieter east coast.
Language
Indonesian is official; Balinese is the everyday local language. English is widely spoken in tourist areas and dive operations.
Currency
Indonesian Rupiah (IDR). Cards are common in resorts; cash is king for small shops and warungs.
Time Zone
WITA (UTC+8), no daylight saving.
Religion
Predominantly Balinese Hindu, the only Hindu-majority province in Muslim-majority Indonesia. Temples, daily offerings, and ceremonies are part of everyday life.
Climate
Tropical, two seasons: dry (roughly April–October) and wet (November–March). Water temps stay warm year-round.
Before You Go

Entry & visa, handled simply

01

Check your passport. Valid at least 6 months beyond your return date.

02

Get your e-VOA before you fly. US citizens need a visa for Indonesia: the Electronic Visa on Arrival (~$35, 30 days, extendable once) lets you skip the airport line. Apply directly through the official government portal: evisa.imigrasi.go.id. That's the only official site; third-party "visa agent" sites often charge inflated fees.

03

File the All Indonesia Arrival Card online, within 3 days before you land. This single form now covers your arrival card, customs declaration, and health declaration together, free and mandatory for every traveler. Official site: allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id.

04

Pay the Bali Tourist Levy, IDR 150,000 (about $10) per person. This is a one-time entry fee the Bali provincial government charges every foreign visitor, it goes toward protecting Bali's environment and culture, not a scam or an airline fee. Pay online in advance at the official site: lovebali.baliprov.go.id. Only use this site, third-party "levy payment" sites are known to overcharge.

05

Non-US passport holders: check with your local Indonesian embassy well in advance, requirements differ by nationality.

Questions

Frequently Asked

Fly into Ngurah Rai International Airport (DPS) in Denpasar, Bali. Airport transfers on arrival and departure are included.

There are no direct flights from Miami to Bali, expect one or two stops and roughly 24 to 30 hours of total travel time. Because Bali runs 12 hours ahead of Miami, you'll typically land two calendar days after you depart, even though you're not actually traveling for two full days. For this trip's start date of Wednesday, August 25, 2027, plan to depart Miami around Monday, August 23, aiming to land in Denpasar (DPS) by early-to-mid afternoon on the 25th so the included airport transfer goes smoothly. Flying from a different city? Use the same math: check your total flight time to Denpasar, then count back using Bali's 12-hour-ahead time difference to land on your target date. This is a planning estimate, not a guaranteed schedule, exact routing varies by airline (common connections run through Doha, Dubai, or Tokyo), so confirm your specific flight's arrival time once you're ready to book.

Yes, US citizens need an Electronic Visa on Arrival (e-VOA) for Indonesia. It's roughly $35, valid 30 days, and you can buy it online ahead of time through the official government portal at evisa.imigrasi.go.id. No need to wait until you land. See "Before You Go" above for the full rundown.

No. This retreat is built to meet you wherever you're starting from, whether you've meditated for years or never sat still for five minutes on purpose.

Snorkeling is offered but optional. Comfort in the water helps, but nobody is required to get in for any activity on this trip.
